title: Dover Records: fair royalties and financial collapse
summary: He offered 10 percent royalties at Dover, but overambition and predatory distributors left him broke from a quarter million dollars in the early 1960s.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Because I only came to that later. You know, when I did Dover Records, for instance, the one thing I wanted to do with Dover Records was give people decent contracts.

Okay? So when I started, you know, it was nothing in those days for me to give people 10% as a starting royalty. Well, let me tell you, all around me I saw people working for 2%, 3%, and 4% and being ripped off for some of that.
You know? And so that was one of the things I thought was wrong and that I tried to correct with Dover Records.

And to whatever extent I did, I did. But I had a lot going there. And because I was overambitious with that, you know, I set, I didn't have any goals. The sky was the limit. I would do anything and everything to do more. So as a concert, I got terribly in debt. And then when I hit a dry period when maybe I didn't have a real hot record those two weeks, and the distributors are all piranhas out there. In those days, they were especially bad, the independent record distributors. That whole thing collapsed on me. I literally lost my ass, you know, including a lot of my own money. Because when I started Dover Records, at that time I was in pretty good shape. I was probably worth, in the early 60s, a minimum of a quarter million dollars. Right. And I blew all of that. When the Dover saga ended, I was busted. You know, I tell people that before the fall, I was driving a Mercedes and my wife was driving a Cadillac. And five years later, we were sharing a Volkswagen. That's as graphic as you can get.
